props.title: Six ways not to, and the one way to.
props.lede: Each tile is the real mark, treated the wrong way. The first is how the site shows it.

tiles.name: As the site shows it
tiles.why: Square, unaltered, on near-black, with room around it.

tiles.name: Stretched
tiles.why: The mark is square. Never squash or widen it.

tiles.name: Recoloured
tiles.why: The red is the red. Do not shift its hue.

tiles.name: Glows and shadows
tiles.why: No effects. The mark is flat.

tiles.name: Crowded
tiles.why: Keep clear space. Nothing should touch or crop it.

tiles.name: Faded
tiles.why: Do not lower its contrast against the ground.

props.title: Where would you lean?
props.lede: Set how much each area of the work draws you. Nothing is stored or sent; it is a mirror, not a form.

axes.label: Interfaces
axes.blurb: Screens that resolve intent in a single read, with motion that explains state.

axes.label: Systems
axes.blurb: Operational platforms, boundaries and the shape of a whole system.

axes.label: Data at scale
axes.blurb: Records in their millions, and the views that make them usable.

axes.label: Engines
axes.blurb: Real-time tools: editors, players and the pipeline between them.

axes.label: Automation
axes.blurb: Work that runs without being asked, and tells you when it can’t.

props.title: Not here? Ask the whole site.
props.lede: Every page’s title and text is searched, with the same engine as ⌘K, and the best answers are laid out below.

props.title: Questions you’re welcome to ask.
props.lede: Eight, on cards. Turn one over to see why it is worth asking, and what a good answer sounds like.

cards.q: What would a good first six months look like?
cards.why: It shows what the company thinks the job is, rather than what the title says.
cards.listen: Specific work and specific outcomes, not adjectives.

cards.q: How are decisions made, and written down?
cards.why: Decisions that are not recorded get made again.
cards.listen: A place where decisions live, and an example of one being reversed.

cards.q: What did the team get wrong recently, and what changed?
cards.why: Teams that can name a recent mistake can learn from one.
cards.listen: A real, recent, specific example, told without blame.

cards.q: Who reviews my work, and how?
cards.why: Review is where you learn the standard.
cards.listen: Named practices, not “we trust each other”.

cards.q: What does support look like at three in the morning?
cards.why: It shows how much thought has gone into running things, not only building them.
cards.listen: Runbooks, ownership, and a view on who should be woken.

cards.q: How do you decide what not to build?
cards.why: Saying no is most of the craft.
cards.listen: Criteria, and a story about something left out.

cards.q: What do you wish candidates asked?
cards.why: It invites the thing they care about most.

cards.q: What would make this a bad fit for me?

props.title: Before a first conversation.
props.lede: Not a form. A sheet of the things worth having to hand, so the first hour is spent on the problem. Tick as you go, copy it, or print it.

items.text: In two sentences: what is going wrong, or what is missing?
Who feels it, and how often?
What happens if nothing changes?
The systems, tools and data involved today
Who owns each of them
Anything that cannot change, and why
What would you see if this had worked?
Who would have to say so?
What would make you stop?
Who can decide, and who only needs to be asked
Anything confidential, and how it may be shared
Dates that are real, and dates that are hopes

props.title: Write it right.
props.lede: Four quick choices. Each is answered the moment you make it.

questions.prompt: The company’s name, on first mention, is…
questions.why: Two words, no hyphen. The site sets it in capitals in places, as a typographic choice, but it is written in sentence case.
“Hanoryx” stands for the company. Initials and abbreviations are not used.
Hanoryx North. It is a team of the company.
It is the company’s own 2D engine, with an editor, a player and export tooling. Only its repository is public.

props.summary: Hanoryx Systems first, Hanoryx after. The team is Hanoryx North. YK Engine is a proprietary 2D engine. No clients, dates or results.

props.title: Take one into your next review.
props.lede: Six cards, one for each principle. Draw one and it comes with a question worth asking out loud.

cards.title: Controlled complexity
cards.question: Which part of this would we be unable to explain in six months, and why are we accepting that?

cards.title: Interfaces before noise
cards.question: What could we take off this screen without anyone noticing it was gone?

cards.title: Motion with purpose
cards.question: What does each movement here say about state, direction or hierarchy? If nothing, why is it moving?

cards.title: Architecture that can expand
cards.question: What would the second use of this look like, and does this design make it cheaper or dearer?

cards.title: Reveal only what is needed
cards.question: Who sees this by default, and who should not?

cards.title: Production-minded prototypes
cards.question: If this prototype were still running in a year, what would break first?

props.title: Send a request through the gates.
props.lede: The four review areas are four questions. Pick a request and watch where, if anywhere, it is turned back.

scenarios.label: A customer reads their own order
scenarios.note: A signed-in customer asks for an order they placed.

scenarios.label: A customer reads someone else’s order
scenarios.note: A signed-in customer asks for an order number that is not theirs.
scenarios.why: The record belongs to someone else, so the read is refused at the service, before any data leaves it.

scenarios.label: A signed-out visitor opens the admin screen
scenarios.why: No identity was presented, so nothing else is even asked.

scenarios.label: A service account exports every record
scenarios.note: A background service asks for everything.
scenarios.why: Its role covers reading one table, not exporting all of them.

scenarios.label: An edit that leaves no trace
scenarios.note: A permitted edit, made through a path that records nothing.
scenarios.why: An action that cannot be traced to an actor and a time is not allowed to complete.

scenarios.label: A support agent refunds an order
scenarios.note: An agent with the refund role acts on a customer’s order.

props.title: Where the story stands.
props.lede: The oldest phase lies deepest; the newest sits just under the surface. Above the line is what has not been told.

phases.name: Foundations
phases.body: Online systems begin beneath the surface: the data model, the boundaries and the roles. The interface comes after the foundations are settled.

phases.name: Coordination
phases.body: An advanced coordination application that brings people, time and information into one shared environment.

phases.name: Customer experience
phases.body: A customer-facing product shaped around the shopping and transaction experience, from first look to confirmation.

phases.name: Data at scale
phases.body: An internal CRM and data system designed for very large data sets — kept internal, and kept quiet.

phases.name: Engine
phases.body: A proprietary 2D engine with an editor, a standalone player and export tooling.

phases.name: Now
phases.body: The company, its work and this site are live. New phases are added here as they are ready to be told.

props.title: Roll the credits.
props.lede: Not people: the disciplines, the work and the parts the company is made from.

props.title: The page you are on, weighed.
props.lede: Its elements, its requests, its size, its first paint and the frame rate it is managing right now. Every number comes from the browser’s own Performance API; nothing is sent anywhere.

props.title: Now try it.
props.lede: Five things worth doing before you go, each a real control: the search, the shortcuts, blueprint mode, the calm setting, and a page chosen for you.

props.title: Open the menu four ways.
props.lede: The same menu, opening on four different curves. Pick the one that feels right, then compare it with the rule of thumb.
props.why: Something that appears in response to a press should start moving at once and settle gently. Ease-out feels immediate; ease-in makes the visitor wait for the movement to begin.

props.title: Write the notice before you break anything.
props.lede: Say what is going, what replaces it and how long people have. Out come the announcement and the two response headers that let tools notice by themselves.

props.title: Write one entry.
props.lede: Fill in the five things a person will want to know. The server’s part — time, request and source — is added for you, and the entry comes out as a line you can copy. Nothing is stored.

props.title: Start the README.
props.lede: Choose the sections that apply. The skeleton is assembled beside you, with a prompt under every heading saying what belongs there. Download it and begin on day one.

sections.name: What it is
sections.prompt: One paragraph: what it does, and who it is for.

sections.name: Run it locally
sections.prompt: The exact commands, from a clean machine to a working copy.

sections.name: Configuration and secrets
sections.prompt: Every setting, what it does, and where its value lives. Never the value itself.

sections.name: How it fits together
sections.prompt: A picture, and a paragraph: the parts, and where they meet.

sections.name: Release and rollback
sections.prompt: How a change reaches production, and how to undo it.

sections.name: Tests
sections.prompt: What runs, how to run it, and what a failure means.

sections.name: Running it
sections.prompt: What is monitored, what the alerts mean, and links to the runbooks.

sections.name: The data
sections.prompt: What each table holds, which are authoritative, and who owns what.

sections.name: Decisions
sections.prompt: Links to the decision records, newest first.

sections.name: Known problems
sections.prompt: What is fragile or wrong, and how to tell when it bites.

sections.name: Who to ask
sections.prompt: Roles and names, and what each can answer.

props.title: Five cards worth keeping.
props.lede: The guide, folded down. Page through them with the arrows, or the arrow keys.

cards.title: Retries are normal
cards.body: Every layer between the person and the database may send a request again. Design for the second copy, not against it.

cards.title: Key the intent
cards.body: The client makes one key per intent, and sends it with every attempt. A new key per attempt recognises nothing.

cards.title: One transaction
cards.body: Keep the key in the same transaction as the effect, with a unique constraint. If they can disagree, they will.

cards.title: Fingerprint it
cards.body: A key is a promise about one request. If it comes back attached to a different one, say so loudly.

cards.title: Test the gap
cards.body: Drop the answer after the commit. Send fifty at once. Kill the process halfway. The bugs live between the steps.

props.title: How far could it reach?
props.lede: Slide to give a job more powers. The ring shows how much a stolen password, or a slip, could touch. The job only ever needed the first three.

powers.name: Read customer records
powers.risk: A stolen key could now read personal data the report never touches.

powers.name: Edit stock levels
powers.risk: A bug, or a thief, could change what the business believes it holds.

powers.name: Create other accounts
powers.risk: An attacker could make themselves a way back in.

powers.name: Change permissions
powers.risk: It could grant itself anything else.

props.title: Which one for this job?
props.lede: Three questions about the job in front of you. The answer names the trigger that fits, and why the others do not.

questions.text: Can one item fail without the others?
options: No — one run covers the lot

100.name: A queue
100.why: Something happened, one worker handles it, and one pass is enough. A queue smooths the burst and keeps the backlog visible.
100.watch: The age of the oldest job, not only the count.

101.name: A queue with retries and a dead-letter queue
101.why: Something happened and each item can fail alone. Give each job a limited number of attempts, then set it aside for a person.
101.watch: A dead-letter queue nobody reads is just a bin.

110.name: Events
110.why: A fact has occurred and several parts need to react, some not yet known. Publish it and let them subscribe.
110.watch: The shape of the event is a contract. Version it.

111.name: Events, with a queue behind each consumer
111.why: A fact, many consumers, and items that can fail alone. Publish the event; give each consumer a queue with its own retries.
111.watch: Replays. Consumers must recognise an event they have already handled.

000.name: Cron
000.why: The clock is the reason, one worker handles it, and one run covers the lot. This is what cron is for.
000.watch: A cron job that silently stops. Add a heartbeat, and skip a run if the last one is still going.

001.name: Cron that feeds a queue
001.why: The time starts it, but each item can fail alone. Let cron decide what is due and put one job per item on a queue.
001.watch: Duplicates: a job can arrive twice. Record what is done in the same transaction as the effect.

010.name: Cron that publishes an event
010.why: The clock starts it, but several parts of the system care. Have the schedule announce a fact, such as “day closed”, and let others react.
010.watch: Consumers that miss the event. Watch each one’s lag.

011.name: A scheduled event, with a queue behind each consumer
011.why: Time starts it, many react, and each item can fail alone. Publish on a schedule, and give each consumer its own queue.
011.watch: A tangle. Name each event as a fact and give it an id.

default.name: A queue
default.why: When in doubt, a queue is the most forgiving: it smooths bursts, retries one item at a time and shows its backlog.
default.watch: Make the work safe to repeat.

props.title: Can’t choose? Spin for one.
props.lede: A reel of the guide titles turns and lands on one. It never lands on the same one twice in a row.

props.title: Draw a figure from a word.
props.lede: A seeded drawing: the same word always makes the same shape, so it is a signature rather than a random picture. Change the rings and spokes, then download it as an SVG.

props.title: Where is the line?
props.lede: Eight things a visitor might do. Decide for each one, then see how the policy reads it.

cases.text: Quote two sentences from a case study in a blog post, with a link back.
cases.why: Short, credited quotation is ordinary use, and linking back is welcome.

cases.text: Run a gentle crawler that identifies itself and respects the robots file.
cases.why: Gentle, identified automated access that follows the robots file is fine.

cases.text: Fetch every page as fast as the connection allows, from several machines at once.
cases.why: That could slow the site for other people. Keep the rate reasonable.

cases.text: Copy the whole site, swap the name, and publish it as your own.
cases.why: Presenting the site’s material as your own is not allowed.

cases.text: Link to the Principles page from a newsletter.
Spot a way to read something that isn’t public, and keep reading it to see how far it goes.
cases.why: Report it instead of using it. The disclosure page says how.

cases.text: Print the privacy notice to PDF and keep it for your records.
cases.why: Printing and saving pages for your own reference is welcome.

cases.text: Register a lookalike domain and email people as “Hanoryx Systems”.
cases.why: Impersonating the company is not allowed, and may be unlawful.

props.title: Tune the site to you.
props.lede: Five settings you can change right now. They apply until you reload and are not stored.

props.title: Follow a report through.
props.lede: Four stages, no promises about how long each takes. Step through to see what happens at each.

stages.label: Received
stages.line: It lands in the company’s mailbox like any email.

stages.label: Read
stages.line: Someone reads it and, if it describes a fault, tries to reproduce it.

stages.label: Answered
stages.line: You are told what was found and what will change, or why nothing will.

stages.label: Followed up
stages.line: The fix goes into the site, and the accessibility statement or documents are updated if they need it.

props.title: Leave nothing behind.
props.lede: One press removes every item this site keeps in your browser. It touches nothing that belongs to another site.

props.title: May I…?
props.lede: Pick what you would like to do. The desk answers in one line, and says what to do next.

cases.label: Link to a page
cases.line: Linking is welcome. Use the page’s own title as the link text.

cases.label: Quote a paragraph
cases.line: Short, credited quotation is ordinary. Say where it came from and link back.

cases.label: Name the company in a talk
cases.line: Referring to the company by name to describe it accurately is fine. Don’t imply endorsement.

cases.label: Show the mark on my site
cases.line: Showing the mark can suggest a connection. Ask first, and say how it will appear.

cases.label: Reuse the site’s code
cases.line: The site’s own code belongs to the company. The third-party libraries under it have their own licences.

cases.label: Copy the whole site
cases.line: Copying the site to publish as your own is not allowed.

cases.label: Use the same typefaces
cases.line: They are open fonts from their designers. Check each licence; none of it is the company’s to grant.

props.title: The fine print, made readable.
props.lede: Move over it. Or switch the lens on, and read it at a size you can.

props.title: Build the link.
props.lede: Pick a page and a format. The link, written the way this policy asks, is ready to copy.

props.title: Your receipt.
props.lede: Everything the site is holding for you right now, itemised from your own browser. Nothing on it was sent anywhere.

props.title: Slide through time.
props.lede: Drag the marker along the ruler, and watch what is still alive at each moment.

stops.label: After you close the tab
stops.note: The browser clears the tab’s storage.

stops.label: A week later
stops.note: Nothing of the site’s remains in your browser.

items.label: Visitor records on the site’s side

props.title: The terms, on one card.
props.lede: Turn it over. One side is what you can do; the other is what not to lean on.
can: Read, use the tools, print what you need
Link to any page, and say where it came from
Quote briefly, as the law allows
Ask to reuse more, through the contact page

Treat a demo or sample record as a real system
Expect the site to always be there, or always right

props.title: Where each document stands.
props.lede: Written, and checked against how the site works. Not yet read by a lawyer.
props.note: The terms and the privacy notice have one open item each: they cannot name the governing law or a registered address until the company’s details are published.

props.title: Write the alt text.
props.lede: Four pictures, four different problems: a chart, an ornament, an icon inside a button and an illustration. Describe each as you would to someone who cannot see it, then check against a few common rules.

props.title: Where does it belong?
props.lede: Eight small responsibilities and four layers. Put each in the layer you would give it, then check against the reasoning. There is rarely only one possible answer; the point is to say why.

layers.name: Interface
layers.blurb: Shows things and takes input. Presentation, and nothing that has to be true.

layers.name: Service surface
layers.blurb: The typed contracts. Who may ask for what, and what shape the question and answer take.

layers.name: Orchestration
layers.blurb: Moves work between states: steps, retries, hand-offs, schedules.

layers.name: Data core
layers.blurb: Owns the truth. One writer per record, with rules that cannot be bypassed.

items.text: Show a price with a currency symbol and two decimals
items.why: Presentation is the edge’s job. The data core stores an amount and a currency code, and every screen formats it for its reader.

items.text: Check that this person may issue a refund
items.why: Authorisation belongs at the boundary of the service, decided there for every request, so no path can skip it.

items.text: Move an order from paid to packed and tell the warehouse
items.why: Moving work between states, and telling other parts about it, is orchestration. State moves; it is not edited loosely.

items.text: Make sure two people cannot change one record at the same moment
items.why: Only the layer that owns the record can guarantee this, with a transaction or a version check that cannot be bypassed.

items.text: Retry a failed email three times, then give up
items.why: Retries, back-off and the point of giving up are about the progress of work, not about data or screens.

items.text: Reject a request that is missing a field it promised to carry
items.why: The contract states the shape of a request. Enforcing it at the surface keeps bad input from travelling any further.

items.text: Remember that this order has been refunded
items.why: A fact about the world is stored where truth lives, once. Everything else reads it.

items.text: Grey out the Refund button for people who cannot refund
items.why: A courtesy at the edge. The real check is at the surface, because anyone can send the request the button would have sent.

props.title: What are you trying to show?
props.lede: Say what the page needs to do and the block that suits it comes up, with the data that makes it and the usual wrong choice.

intents.label: One thing that must not be missed
intents.sees: A note, a tip, a warning
intents.why: It sets one remark apart from the text, worded by kind so that colour is never the only signal.
intents.notThis: A banner across the whole site for something that belongs to one page.

intents.label: Records people will compare
intents.why: A table is the honest shape for records. A screen reader can say which column a cell is in, and a sortable header lets people put the rows in their own order.
intents.notThis: A grid of cards, which hides the columns and with them the comparison.
intents.sample:
{
  type: 'table',
  caption: 'Scheduled jobs',
  head: ['Job', 'Minutes'],
  rows: [['Nightly export', '12'], ['Archive old records', '48']],
  sortable: true,
}

intents.label: Things in an order
intents.why: An ordered list, so the order is announced. Words such as First and Then do the job of dates, and they are never wrong.
intents.notThis: Dates the page cannot back up.

intents.label: Questions people ask
intents.why: Each answer is a disclosure, so a long page of questions stays easy to scan and a closed answer is out of the tab order and the reading order.
intents.notThis: A wall of text with the questions in bold.

intents.label: Two ways of doing it
intents.why: Columns that say in words what each side is, so the comparison does not depend on colour.
intents.notThis: A table of ticks and crosses, which says less and reads worse aloud.

intents.label: A piece of code or data
intents.sees: Text that must be copied exactly
intents.why: It keeps every character, offers a copy button and can be scrolled from the keyboard. The colours are a nicety; copying gives exactly what you see.
intents.notThis: A screenshot of code, which cannot be copied, searched or read aloud.

intents.label: Several short views of one thing
intents.why: One panel at a time, with the arrow keys moving between the tabs and the panel shown at once.
intents.notThis: Tabs for things a reader must compare, which hide one half of the comparison.

intents.label: The company’s own words
intents.why: A real blockquote with its source as the caption. It is for words someone said and agreed to have quoted.

intents.label: A list to tick through
intents.why: Real checkboxes, with a count that is announced politely. The ticks live in the page and nothing is stored.
intents.notThis: A numbered list, which shows an order but not how far you have got.

intents.label: Facts about one thing
intents.why: A real description list, so a screen reader pairs each term with its detail.
intents.notThis: Bold text and a colon, which looks the same and means nothing to software.

intents.label: Where to go next
intents.why: Cards that each hold one link, so the thing you press is a link with a name and not a whole card wrapped in an anchor.
intents.notThis: A row of bare addresses, or “click here”.

intents.label: A few figures
intents.why: Each figure is large and labelled, and how it moved is said in words as well as drawn. A note says where the figures come from.
intents.notThis: A figure with no baseline and no source.

props.tag: End of the content and layout components
props.title: Set a reading column.
props.lede: Slide the measure, the line height and the size, and change the face. The text reflows as you go, and the page says whether each setting is short, comfortable or long: the rules of thumb behind the Prose component.
props.heading: Handing a system over
paragraphs: A handover is judged by the first change a stranger can make safely. Everything else — the diagrams, the wiki, the recorded walkthrough — is in service of that one moment, and it is worth designing for it from the first week rather than the last.

The people who built a system carry a great deal in their heads: why a table is shaped as it is, which job must never run twice, what the odd configuration value is for. None of it is secret, and almost none of it is written down. The work of a handover is the unglamorous work of writing it down while it is still fresh.
Write how it is run, not only how it is built. List what can go wrong, in the order it usually does. Say what you would do differently. A newcomer reading that has a head start of months.

props.tag: End of the data display components
props.title: What shape is your data?
props.lede: Choose the shape the information has and the page shows the component that suits it, drawn with sample data, with the reason — and the usual wrong choice and why it fails.

shapes.label: A trend over time
shapes.why: A single line shows direction at a glance and takes almost no room, so it fits in a row, a card or a sentence. Give it a text description so the shape is never the only way in.
shapes.notThis: A full chart with axes, gridlines and a legend, when all anyone needs is better or worse.

shapes.label: A few values to compare
shapes.sees: Four or five things, one measure
shapes.why: Length is the easiest thing for the eye to compare, and a list keeps the label and the figure beside the bar, so the numbers stay real text.
shapes.notThis: A pie or donut. Angles and areas are hard to compare, and the labels end up far from the slices.

shapes.label: Records with several fields
shapes.why: When people need to find, sort and compare rows, a table is the honest shape. Headers are real headers, so a screen reader can say which column a cell is in.
shapes.notThis: A grid of cards. Cards hide the columns, and with them the ability to compare.

shapes.label: Facts about one thing
shapes.why: A term and its detail, paired in the markup and not only side by side on the screen.
shapes.notThis: Bold text and a colon in a paragraph. It looks the same and means nothing to software.

shapes.label: Things in an order
shapes.why: An ordered list, so the order is announced. The line and the markers only repeat what the list already says.
shapes.notThis: Dates you do not have. If the order is known and the dates are not, say phases — this site does.

shapes.label: Things inside things
shapes.why: One tab stop, arrow keys to walk it, and the level and position announced for every item.
shapes.notThis: Nested lists of links where every item is a tab stop: forty Tabs to get past a folder.

shapes.label: One important number
shapes.why: Large, labelled and, if you have it, compared with something — in words.
shapes.notThis: A gauge, when a number would do.

props.title: Fire one, and read what it says.
props.lede: Toasts for what needs no answer, alerts for what needs looking at. Each time you fire one, the log writes down the words a screen reader would say and whether it would wait politely or interrupt.

presets.label: Copied
presets.title: Copied
presets.body: The address is on your clipboard.

presets.label: Syncing
presets.title: Syncing
presets.body: This can take a moment. You can keep working.

presets.label: Failed
presets.title: Could not save
presets.body: Check your connection and try again.

alerts.label: Information
alerts.title: Maintenance window
alerts.body: The service is read-only from 02:00 to 02:30 UTC on Sunday.

alerts.label: Error
alerts.title: Export failed
alerts.body: Two rows had no order number.

props.title: Build a form, check it, take the code.
props.lede: Tick the fields a form needs and the page builds it from the kit’s own components. Send it empty to see how the errors read and where focus goes; the JSX underneath is yours to copy.

fields.label: Password
fields.hint: At least 12 characters is a good start.

props.title: Walk a flow, and hear it.
props.lede: Four steps with a stepper, a Next that waits until the step is complete and says why, and focus that moves to each step’s heading. Beside it, a log writes down what a screen reader would announce.

steps.title: Details
steps.intro: Give it a name. At least three characters unlocks the next step.

steps.title: Review
steps.intro: Read back what you entered. Nothing has happened yet.

steps.title: Confirm
steps.intro: One last check before it would be made.

props.title: Try to escape the dialog.
props.lede: Open it and press Tab, Shift+Tab and Escape. A log beside it writes down where focus goes: in, round and round inside, and back to the button that opened it.
rules: Focus moves in when it opens, to the first control or the one marked for it.
Tab and Shift+Tab cycle inside; focus never reaches the page behind.
Escape, the close button and a press on the dark area all dismiss it.
Focus returns to what opened it, and the page behind stops scrolling meanwhile.

props.title: Which component do you need?
props.lede: Say what you are trying to do, then narrow it. The page names the one or two components that fit, says why, and takes you to each in its gallery.

choices.label: A few words or a number

picks.why: One line with a label, a hint and an error that is announced. Add a prefix or suffix for a unit.
If it is a quantity with a range: arrows step it, typing is free, and it is clamped when you leave.
Native radios: the arrows choose, and a screen reader says “2 of 4”.
When the choices are short and few and the control should read as one piece.
Native, so a phone gives its own picker. The first thing to try.
When the list is long enough that people will want to type to find their answer.
Each option is its own box; a parent box can show the mixed state.
When people supply their own words rather than choosing from a list.
Drag and drop, with a real file button underneath for everyone else.
A trail back up the site, with the current page marked.
For a long page: the section you are in is marked as you read.
The steps in order and which one you are on, written out for a screen reader.
For a long list split into pages: first, last and the neighbours.
When each choice shows a different panel of content.
When each choice only changes a setting or a nearby demonstration.
A button that opens a menu of actions, with typeahead and Escape.
A row of tools that is one tab stop, with toggles.

choices.label: List the pages of a section

picks.why: Grouped links that fold, with the current page marked.
A brief message in a corner that leaves by itself and never takes focus.
A live state, written out beside its colour.

choices.label: It is about this part of the page

picks.why: In the flow, with a tone that is also an icon and a word.

choices.label: It is about the whole page

picks.why: Runs the width of its container, with one action and a dismiss.
When the wait is short and you cannot say how short.
When you know the shape of what is coming and want nothing to jump.
When you know how far along it is.
Say why, and say what to do next.
Sortable, selectable, and scrollable inside a named region.
Labels and values, paired in the markup.
For the one number that matters, with how it moved.
Direction at a glance, with a text description of the range.
Length is easy to compare, and the figures stay as text.
One quantity inside a known range, with its zone in words.
An ordered list with a line and markers.
One tab stop, arrow keys to walk it.
With a copy button, optional line numbers and light colouring.

choices.label: A hint on hover or focus

picks.why: A short description that adds detail and never replaces a label.
A richer preview of where a link goes.
Opens under a button; not modal, so Tab moves on.
Takes over until it is dealt with; traps focus and gives it back.
For “are you sure?”, with buttons that say what they do.
A dialog that runs the full height from an edge.
A surface with an eyebrow, a heading and a foot.
A remark set apart from the text: a note, a tip, a warning.
A column with an even gap.
A row that wraps.
As many columns as fit, with no breakpoint.
A reading column about 68 characters wide.
A pull quote with its source.
A picture and its caption, kept together.
One section that opens and closes properly.

choices.label: Hold the shape of an image

picks.why: Reserves the room before the picture arrives.

props.title: Change a decision. Watch it spread.
props.lede: Five tokens on a small interface: an accent colour, a corner radius, a space unit, a transition time and a base text size. Change one and everything that uses it follows. The values are set on the preview alone.

props.title: Review this change.
props.lede: Twelve lines that charge a customer. Read them the way a reviewer would and mark the ones you would not let through. There are four real problems and eight lines that are fine.

flaw.title: No timeout
flaw.why: If the provider never answers, this waits for ever, and so does the customer. Every outbound call needs a limit and a decision about what happens when it is reached.

flaw.title: A secret in the code
flaw.why: Anything in the repository is readable by everyone who can read it, for as long as history is kept. Secrets belong in the environment and can be changed without a release.

flaw.title: No idempotency key
flaw.why: A retry after a lost answer will charge twice. Send a key derived from the order so the provider can recognise a repeat.

flaw.title: Success assumed
flaw.why: Nothing checks res.ok. A declined card or a server error comes back as data, and the next line treats it as success.

props.title: Write your definition of done.
props.lede: Choose what must be true before work counts as finished. The list becomes a card to print or paste. Keep it short enough that it is really checked.

items.text: It does what the problem statement asked, and nothing it was told to leave out.
The unhappy paths have been decided and tried, not only the happy one.
It is as small as it can be while still being a whole change.
The automated checks pass on the branch.
New behaviour has a test that would fail without it.
It has been used with a keyboard alone.
Someone other than the author has read it and said so.
Every blocker has been answered, and nits are decided either way.
It has been released, and the way back has been checked.
It has been watched for a while after release.
Monitoring or alerts have been updated if the change needed it.
The README and any runbook the change touches are up to date.
A decision record exists if the choice would surprise a newcomer.
One line is in the release notes, in plain words.

props.title: Every control owns seven states.
props.lede: Resting, hover, focus, pressed, disabled, busy and error, side by side for a button, a field and a switch. Underneath is the real thing: hover it, Tab to it, press it.

props.title: One menu, three policies.
props.lede: The same menu opening in full, in calm and in still. The site follows the device’s reduced-motion setting, and also offers a calm display setting of its own, which stills the drawn backgrounds.

props.title: Break it on purpose.
props.lede: Spin the wheel for a way things go wrong, read what should happen, and how to rehearse it. Mark the ones you have actually tried.

scenarios.name: A dependency is down
scenarios.happens: A service you call stops answering, or answers slowly.
scenarios.should: The page says so plainly, the rest of it keeps working, and the call gives up after a sensible time.
scenarios.test: Point the call at an address that never answers. Does anything hang? Is the message honest?

scenarios.name: The same request arrives twice
scenarios.happens: A person double-clicks, or a network retries.
scenarios.should: One effect, and the same answer both times.
scenarios.test: Send the request twice at once, and twice with the answer thrown away between.

scenarios.name: The input is enormous
scenarios.happens: Someone pastes a million characters, or uploads a vast file.
scenarios.should: It is refused clearly, quickly and without taking the server down.
scenarios.test: Send a body many times larger than any real one and watch memory and time.

scenarios.name: The list is empty
scenarios.happens: No orders, no results, no messages yet.
scenarios.should: A page that explains the emptiness and what to do about it, not a blank or an error.
scenarios.test: Open every list with no data. Look at the words as well as the layout.

scenarios.name: The clock jumps
scenarios.happens: Daylight saving changes, or a server’s time is corrected.
scenarios.should: Schedules run once, durations stay positive and times are stored in UTC.
scenarios.test: Run the scheduling code with the clock set to the hour before a change.

scenarios.name: The disk fills up
scenarios.happens: Logs or uploads use every last byte.
scenarios.should: Writes fail loudly, alerts fire and nothing is silently lost.
scenarios.test: Fill a small disk in a test environment and watch what breaks first.

scenarios.name: The network is slow
scenarios.happens: A phone on a weak connection, a long way from the server.
scenarios.should: Something useful appears early, and nothing jumps around as the rest arrives.
scenarios.test: Throttle the connection in the browser’s tools and load the heaviest page.

scenarios.name: Someone changes an id
scenarios.happens: A person edits the number in an address to see what is next.
scenarios.should: They see only what they are allowed to, and learn nothing about what exists.
scenarios.test: Sign in as one user and request another user’s record by id.

props.title: Pull one out.
props.lede: Choose a part of the stack and take it away in your head. The card says what stops, what carries on and what it would cost to replace. The judgements are ours.

parts.name: lenis
parts.headline: Scrolling would be the browser’s own.
parts.stops: The smooth, eased scrolling and the glide to a section when a link points at one.
parts.keeps: Every page, every link and all content. Scroll-linked effects would still read the scroll position.
parts.how: It lives behind one provider and one hook. Change what the hook returns and the callers carry on.

parts.name: gsap
parts.headline: The timelines and the pointer-driven effects go.
parts.stops: The intro sequence, the custom cursor, magnetic buttons, the title that answers the pointer and the marquee that scroll speed pushes.
parts.keeps: Content, routing, layout and the canvases. The entrance reveals use the other animation library and would carry on.
parts.how: Each effect is its own component. They could be dropped one by one, or rewritten with CSS and the other library.

parts.name: motion
parts.headline: Things would arrive and change without easing.
parts.stops: The entrance reveals as sections scroll into view, page transitions, and the springs and glides in menus, tabs and panels.
parts.keeps: All content and function. Controls would still work, and change state at once.
parts.how: It is used widely. Most uses could become CSS transitions or animations; the layout transitions are the hard part.

parts.name: react-router-dom
parts.headline: There would be one page.
parts.stops: Every page address, every link between pages and the back button’s meaning.
parts.keeps: Components and styles. The content would have nowhere to be addressed.
parts.how: Routing is the skeleton of the site. Replacing it with another router is realistic; removing it is not.

parts.name: lucide-react
parts.headline: The small line icons disappear.
parts.stops: Arrows, chevrons, and the pictograms on buttons and cards.
parts.keeps: All text and behaviour. Controls keep their labels.
parts.how: Replace with inline SVGs, one icon at a time. Tedious rather than hard.

parts.name: clsx
parts.headline: Class names would be joined by hand.
parts.stops: Nothing visible; a convenience for conditional class names.
parts.how: It does one tiny job; template strings could do it, at the price of tidiness.

parts.name: The canvas scenes
parts.headline: The backgrounds would be plain.
parts.stops: The animated backgrounds behind every section and hero.
parts.keeps: All content and function. Calm mode already shows pages without moving backgrounds.
parts.how: Sections declare a scene by name. Removing them leaves a quiet page that works.

props.title: Assemble a pipeline.
props.lede: Choose the checks, put them in order, and a workflow file comes out, with the same sequence as a local script. The commands are placeholders for your own project’s.

props.title: What is going wrong?
props.lede: Start from the symptom, not from what the team is called. Choose the one that sounds most like yours and the page names the discipline that deals with it, and why.

symptoms.label: The numbers disagree between screens
symptoms.why: Two places think they own the same fact. The fix is one source of truth per record and one writer, with everything else reading through a contract.

symptoms.label: People avoid using it
symptoms.why: Usually the controls do not say what they are, what state they are in or what will happen. Components with a job, and every state shown, are the cure.

symptoms.label: It feels laggy or jumpy
symptoms.why: Something is spending more than its share of each frame. A motion budget says what can move, how much and on which property.

symptoms.label: It breaks, and we find out late
symptoms.why: The checks are missing, or they are the wrong kind. Layer cheap fast checks in front of slow broad ones, and watch the quiet failures.

symptoms.label: Nobody dares change it
symptoms.why: Changes are too big to understand and too hard to undo. Small steps with gates between them make change safe again.

symptoms.label: It is slow to start
symptoms.why: Too much is shipped before anything shows. Splitting by page and loading only what a page uses is a matter of structure, not tuning.

symptoms.label: Some people cannot use it
symptoms.why: Structure, keyboard, contrast and choice. Look at the page the way a screen reader does, and fix what it meets.

symptoms.label: We cannot see what it is doing
symptoms.why: There is no view of the layers. Tracing a page view through them, and measuring it, is how a team learns what its system is really doing.

props.title: The whole history in one chart.
props.lede: A row for each chapter, a bar as long as the notes in it, cut into what was added, changed and fixed. Point at a row for the chapter; press it to read.

props.title: Join several into one.
props.lede: Choose documents and have them joined into a single Markdown file with a contents list: a pack for a new project, a new teammate, or a handover.

props.title: Test yourself.
props.lede: Ten flashcards, dealt from the glossary. Read the term, say what it means, turn the card, and mark whether you had it.

props.title: Grade a whole palette.
props.lede: Paste the colours you are working with. Every text-on-background pairing is graded in a grid, so the ones that never work are visible before anything is designed with them.

props.title: The day the clock lies.
props.lede: Choose a zone and a time of day. The page finds the days this year when the clocks change there, and says what happens to your time on each: skipped, repeated, or fine.

props.title: Imagine it went badly.
props.lede: A pre-mortem: it is a year later and the decision turned out badly. Why? Write the reasons, how likely each is, and what you would do about it now. The riskiest come out first.

props.title: The launch fortnight.
props.lede: Seven stops from two weeks before to a week after. Walk along the track, tick what you have done at each stop, and watch the ring fill. The arrow keys move between stops.

stops.title: Two weeks out: decide, and find the gaps
items: Name the person who decides go or no-go
Run the readiness check and write down the gaps
Rehearse a restore of the backup, and time it

stops.title: A week out: test the riskiest path
items: Walk the riskiest path from end to end
Have someone who did not write them follow the runbooks
Confirm who is on call, and how they are reached

stops.title: Three days out: freeze and rehearse
items: Freeze changes that are not needed for the launch
Break something on purpose, to see that monitoring notices
Tell the people who will be affected, and when

stops.title: The day before: confirm the way back
items: Confirm the rollback, and who may call it
Check capacity against the load you expect
Agree the plan for the first hour

stops.title: Launch day: release quietly, watch together
items: Release in a quiet hour, not a busy one
Watch the first-hour graphs together
Write down anything odd as it happens

stops.title: The day after: review and mend
items: Read the overnight alerts
Fix the small things while the memory is fresh
Thank the people who stayed up

stops.title: A week after: learn from it
items: Hold a blameless review
Update the runbooks with what you learned
Decide what to leave alone

props.title: Make one size fluid.
props.lede: Give a smallest and a largest size, and the window widths between which it grows. One line of CSS comes out, with no media query. Drag the slider to stand in for the browser window.

props.title: All five, on one page.
props.lede: The thresholds, the ratios, the field ranges, the groups and the headings the tools turn on, laid out as a sheet. Print it, or copy it as plain text.

props.title: Make a reading list.
props.lede: Tick pages from anywhere on the site, or start from a preset. The list comes out as Markdown, with the links and an estimate of the time, ready to send to someone.

props.title: Is it worth automating?
props.lede: How long the job takes, how often it happens, what it costs to build and what it costs to keep alive. The page says when it pays for itself, if it ever does. Your numbers; only the arithmetic is ours.

props.title: How big is yours?
props.lede: Five questions about a system, each a judgement. The answer is a shape, not a price and not a duration: what kind of work this adds up to, what changes at that size and what to decide first.

questions.text: How many kinds of people use it?
How many other systems does it talk to?
What happens if it is down for a day?

options.label: Money or safety is at risk

questions.text: Where does its data come from?

options.label: We migrate from systems still in use

bands.name: A focused tool
bands.summary: One job, a few people, little around it. It can be small, quick and simple, and should stay that way.
changes: One person can hold the whole thing in their head.
A single release path is enough.
A good README is the documentation.
first: The one job it must do well.

bands.name: A platform
bands.summary: Several roles and several neighbours. The seams between the parts now matter as much as the parts.
changes: Boundaries and contracts between parts become the design.
Access rules need to be written down and tested.
Operation (watching, alerting, recovering) is part of the build.
first: Who may see and do what.
What the source of truth is for each record.
How you will know when it is unwell.

bands.name: A programme
bands.summary: Many roles, sensitive data and real consequences if it stops. A long piece of work with several parts moving together, which has to be managed as one.
changes: Work is staged, with a working slice early.
Security, audit and recovery are designed first, not added.
Several people must be able to run it, so handover starts in week one.
Migration and running in parallel are projects of their own.
first: The riskiest assumption, and how to test it first.
What must never be lost, and how it is protected.
How you will cut over, and how you will go back.

props.title: Design what the customer sees.
props.lede: Ten fields of an invented order. Each says what the usual rule is. Switch them on and off, and the preview changes, with a warning for anything that should never leave the building.

fields.label: Order status
fields.why: The thing they came to find out.

fields.label: What they ordered
fields.why: They chose it. Show it back.

fields.label: What they paid
fields.why: Their own money, on their own order.

fields.label: Tracking number
fields.why: Helps them, and costs nothing to share.

fields.label: Delivery address
fields.why: Theirs to see, and never anyone else’s: show it only to the signed-in owner.

fields.label: Email on file
fields.why: Fine for them to see. A leak if it reaches the wrong visitor.

fields.label: Margin on the order
fields.why: Internal. It says what the business earns.

fields.label: Internal notes
fields.why: Written for colleagues, in a tone not meant for the customer.

fields.label: Support agent
fields.why: A colleague’s identity is theirs to share, not the system’s.

fields.label: Fraud score
fields.why: Showing it teaches people to game it.

props.title: Two people, one item left.
props.lede: The classic race: both press Buy at the same moment. Step through three ways of handling it and see which of them sell the item twice.

props.title: One record, four people.
props.lede: Each role needs a few of the fields and not the rest. Choose a role and the record rearranges itself: what they need is sharp, what they do not is tucked away but never gone. An invented record.

roles.name: Support
roles.asks: Where is it, and what did they pay?

roles.name: Finance
roles.asks: What came in, and what went back?

roles.name: Warehouse
roles.asks: What goes in the box, and where does it go?

props.title: Write the contract.
props.lede: Choose what is sent, when, what happens when it fails and who owns it. Out comes a one-page contract to put in front of both teams. It is a starting point to adapt, not a legal document.

props.title: Where did that number come from?
props.lede: Press the figure and follow it down, hop by hop, to the system that produced it, seeing what must be recorded at each hop for the trail to be walkable. The figure is invented, to show the idea.

hops.name: A figure on a screen
hops.says: The number someone is about to act on.
hops.record: Which query produced it, which version of that query, and when it last ran.

hops.name: A query over cleaned records
hops.says: Counts refunds against orders for the period, leaving out test orders.
hops.record: The exact definition: what counts as a refund, what counts as an order, which dates.

hops.name: Tidied, de-duplicated rows
hops.says: Orders and refunds after the rules that tidy them: repeats removed, currencies converted.
hops.record: Every rule applied, with a count of the rows each one changed or dropped.

hops.name: What happened, in order
hops.says: Each refund as it was requested, approved and paid.
hops.record: Who did it, when, and a reason or a ticket reference.

hops.name: The system where it really happened
hops.says: The payment provider’s record and the shop’s own database, where the money and the order actually changed.
hops.record: The provider’s own reference, so that a person can open the original.

props.title: Plan the end now.
props.lede: Choose what applies to a system you might one day retire, and how much notice people get. Out comes an ordered plan, counted back from the day it is switched off.

items.text: Tell everyone who uses it, and say what replaces it.
Give people a place to ask questions.
Remind them again, closer to the day.
Offer every user an export of their own data.
Decide what must be kept, and for how long.
Move or archive what must be kept, and check that it can be read.
Delete what must not be kept, and record that you did.
List every integration that talks to it.
Tell the owners of those integrations.
Revoke accounts, keys and tokens.
Remove service accounts and firewall rules.
Put a notice page where it used to be.
Redirect old addresses to what replaces them.
Watch for requests still arriving.
Write down why it was retired and what was learned.
Archive the documentation and decision records.
Update the list of systems the company runs.
Cancel hosting, licences and domains, in that order.
Confirm the final bill.

props.title: Find the slowest step.
props.lede: Five steps, each with people and minutes per item. The slowest is marked, and adding a person anywhere else changes nothing. An invented operation, to show the shape.

props.title: Write the hypothesis down.
props.lede: A small card for a small experiment. A good hypothesis can be wrong, says what would show it, and says when to stop. Fill the five lines; the page flags the usual weaknesses, and the card can be taken away.

props.title: Write the brief first.
props.lede: Six short answers about an operation become a one-page brief you can keep, share or bring to a first conversation. It is the sheet the first conversation needs, written before the conversation. Nothing is sent anywhere.

props.title: In scope, and out.
props.lede: The centre is what this policy covers. Every ring beyond it belongs to someone else.

rings.label: The website
rings.note: The site at its public address.
items: Pages, scripts and styles
Links, redirects and addresses
What the site’s code sends, and to whom

rings.label: How it is delivered
rings.note: How the site reaches your browser, as far as the company controls it.
items: Headers and settings the company chooses
The way files are served from the site’s host

rings.label: Services it depends on
rings.note: Other people’s systems. Report problems to their owners.
items: The hosting platform
The font service
GitHub

rings.label: People and places
rings.note: Not covered by this policy at all.
items: Social engineering of the company’s people
Physical attacks
Denial of service

props.title: The whole list, as a file.
props.lede: Built on the spot from the same data as the table above. Read it here, copy it, or take it with you.

props.title: The tape keeps running.
props.lede: Every frame this page draws is a column below. Move, scroll, and watch what it costs.

props.title: Where has this tab been?
props.lede: Read from the browser’s own record of the requests this tab made, grouped by host and matched against the list above.

expected.fonts.googleapis.com: The typeface styles — Google Fonts, listed above.
expected.fonts.gstatic.com: The typeface files — Google Fonts, listed above.

props.title: Don’t take our word for it.
props.lede: Four checks that run on this page, in your browser, and say what they find.

props.title: Every step has a price.
props.lede: Every step between a first look and a confirmed purchase takes some people away. Set how many carry on at each step (the numbers start invented) and watch the losses multiply; then take a step away and see what it was worth.

props.title: The six questions, put to ours.
props.lede: For each of the four pieces of work on this site, which of the six questions are answered, which only partly, and which are not said at all. Written plainly, because the gaps are the point.

questions.why: A named client, a kind of client, or no one in particular?
The question case studies exist to answer.
A number, a comparison, a person.

questions.text: What went wrong, or was hard?
questions.why: Every project had a bad week.

who.text: Described by purpose, as a coordination application for people, time and information. No customer is named.

what.text: Scheduling, communication and records in one environment, with access scoped to each role.

wrong.text: Not covered. The page describes the work; it is not a post-mortem.

look.text: Three small experiments with the idea behind it are on the page. They are not the application.

who.text: Not stated. The page says what the engine is, not who uses it.

what.text: A 2D engine with an editor, a standalone player and project export tooling.

know.text: The page’s own frame-time graph is measured live from the demonstration in your browser, not from the engine.

look.text: A public repository, linked from the page. The editor and player on the page are illustrations.

who.text: A customer-facing product around shopping and transactions. Unnamed by design.

what.text: The path from a first look to a confirmed purchase, described in five frames.

look.text: Described, not displayed. The page shows abstract wireframes, not screenshots, and says so. The product is not public.

who.text: An internal system, for the people who run an operation. Not a public product.

what.text: Designed for very large data sets. The page demonstrates the idea with synthetic rows made in your browser; no speed or size of the real system is claimed.

look.text: Internal by design. It is not public.

props.title: Finding one row among millions.
props.lede: Three ways, with the number of steps each takes as the table grows. Then the real thing: the page builds half a million rows in your browser and times each method for you.

props.title: Why one shared picture.
props.lede: Everyone telling everyone needs a channel for every pair of people, and that count grows with the square of the headcount. One shared picture needs one per person. The arithmetic, drawn.

props.title: Why engines fix the step.
props.lede: The same ball dropped three ways: with a tiny step, with a fixed step that catches up however slowly frames arrive, and with whatever time the last frame took. An illustration of the idea, not the engine’s own code.

props.title: Put any two side by side.
props.lede: Choose two of the four. The rows are the things the work pages say; where a row is the same for both it is marked, because what two pieces of work share is as telling as how they differ.
